entry.sum: A function $f\colon A \to B$ assigns to every input $x$ in its domain $A$ exactly one output $f(x)$. Its graph, the set of points $(x, f(x))$, turns algebraic properties into pictures. The idea to remember is one output per input, which is why a vertical line meets a graph at most once.
key: f\colon A \to B,\quad x \mapsto f(x)
y = f(x - h) + k \text{ is the graph of } y = f(x) \text{ moved } h \text{ right and } k \text{ up}
(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)), \qquad f^{-1} \text{ exists} \iff f \text{ is a bijection}
entry.why: Every quantity that depends on another, such as a fare depending on distance or a position depending on time, is a function. Calculus, algebra and probability are all written in this language.

links.note: A program that returns one output for each input computes a function, and the injective maps are exactly the encodings that can be decoded without loss.
Physical laws are stated as functions, such as position as a function of time or pressure as a function of volume.
Linear maps are the functions between vector spaces that respect addition and scaling, and matrices are how they are written down.

refs: Gelfand, Glagoleva & Shnol, Functions and Graphs

blocks.body:
A taxi fare depends on the distance driven; the temperature depends on the time of day. In each case one quantity determines another, and a function is the mathematical name for such a rule.

This lesson defines functions, reads their properties from graphs, moves graphs around, and shows how functions are combined and undone.

blocks.title: Function
blocks.body:
Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. A function $f$ from $A$ to $B$, written $f\colon A \to B$, is a rule that assigns to each element $x \in A$ exactly one element $f(x) \in B$. The set $A$ is the domain of $f$ and $B$ is its codomain. The set of values actually taken,
$$f(A) = \{ f(x) : x \in A \},$$
is the range (or image) of $f$.

In short: every input gets an output, and no input gets two.

blocks.title: Domain, range and graph
blocks.body:
When a function is given by a formula and nothing else is said, its domain is all real $x$ for which the formula makes sense: every $x \ne 2$ for $\dfrac{1}{x - 2}$, and $x \ge 1$ for $\sqrt{x - 1}$, since negative numbers have no real square root.

The range is often harder. For $h(x) = x^2 + 1$, every value is at least $1$ because $x^2 \ge 0$, and every $y \ge 1$ is reached, at $x = \sqrt{y - 1}$. So the range is $[1, \infty)$. Finding a range means asking for which $y$ the equation $f(x) = y$ has a solution in the domain.

The graph of $f$ is the set of points $(x, f(x))$ with $x$ in the domain. One output per input means that every vertical line meets a graph at most once; so the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ is not a graph, though its upper half is the graph of $\sqrt{1 - x^2}$.

Begin a sketch with a table of values. For $f(x) = x^2 - 2x - 3$:
$$\begin{array}{c|ccccccc} x & -2 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline f(x) & 5 & 0 & -3 & -4 & -3 & 0 & 5 \end{array}$$
The values fall and then rise, symmetrically about $x = 1$, with zeros at $-1$ and $3$. Indeed $f(x) = (x + 1)(x - 3) = (x - 1)^2 - 4$: a parabola with lowest point $(1, -4)$.

blocks.title: Reading a graph
blocks.body:
Several properties have both an algebraic definition and a picture.

- $f$ is increasing on an interval if $x_1 < x_2$ implies $f(x_1) < f(x_2)$ there: the graph rises from left to right. Decreasing: $x_1 < x_2$ implies $f(x_1) > f(x_2)$.
- A zero of $f$ is an $x$ with $f(x) = 0$, where the graph meets the $x$-axis.
- $f$ is even if $f(-x) = f(x)$ for all $x$ in the domain: the graph is symmetric in the $y$-axis, as for $x^2$ and $|x|$.
- $f$ is odd if $f(-x) = -f(x)$ for all $x$ in the domain: the graph is unchanged by a half turn about the origin, as for $x^3$ and $1/x$.

Most functions are neither, but if the domain is symmetric about $0$, then
$$f(x) = \frac{f(x) + f(-x)}{2} + \frac{f(x) - f(-x)}{2}$$
writes $f$ as an even function plus an odd one. For instance $x^2 - 2x - 3$ has even part $x^2 - 3$ and odd part $-2x$.

blocks.title: Moving and stretching graphs
blocks.body:
Suppose you know the graph of $y = f(x)$. With $h, k$ real and $a > 0$:

1. $y = f(x) + k$: shift up by $k$.
2. $y = f(x - h)$: shift right by $h$.
3. $y = a f(x)$: stretch vertically by the factor $a$.
4. $y = f(x/a)$: stretch horizontally by the factor $a$.
5. $y = -f(x)$: reflect in the $x$-axis; $y = f(-x)$: reflect in the $y$-axis.

Rule 2 surprises people: a minus sign moves the graph right. The reason is that $f(x - h)$ takes at $x_0 + h$ the value $f(x_0)$, which $f$ took at $x_0$.

Completing the square uses these rules. Since $2x^2 - 12x + 19 = 2(x - 3)^2 + 1$, the graph of $y = 2x^2 - 12x + 19$ is the parabola $y = x^2$ stretched vertically by $2$, moved $3$ right and $1$ up. Its lowest point is $(3, 1)$ and its range is $[1, \infty)$.

blocks.title: Composition and inverse
blocks.body:
If $f\colon A \to B$ and $g\colon B \to C$, the composition $g \circ f\colon A \to C$ is defined by $(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))$: first apply $f$, then $g$.

A function $g\colon B \to A$ is an inverse of $f\colon A \to B$ if $g(f(x)) = x$ for every $x \in A$ and $f(g(y)) = y$ for every $y \in B$. When it exists it is written $f^{-1}$.

blocks.title: Composing and undoing
blocks.body:
Order matters in composition. With $f(x) = x + 1$ and $g(x) = x^2$, $(g \circ f)(x) = (x + 1)^2$ but $(f \circ g)(x) = x^2 + 1$; at $x = 1$ these are $4$ and $2$.

A function composed with itself can surprise. Let $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{1 - x}$ for $x \ne 1$. For $x \ne 0, 1$,
$$f(f(x)) = \frac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{1 - x}} = \frac{x - 1}{x}, \qquad f(f(f(x))) = \frac{1}{1 - \frac{x - 1}{x}} = x.$$
Three applications of $f$ bring every number except $0$ and $1$ back to where it started ($f(0) = 1$ and $f(1)$ is undefined).

To undo $f$, different inputs must give different outputs, and every element of $B$ must be an output. So: $f$ is injective (one-to-one) if $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$ implies $x_1 = x_2$; for a real function, every horizontal line meets the graph at most once. $f$ is surjective (onto) if its range is all of $B$. A function that is both is a bijection.

blocks.title: Inverses exist exactly for bijections
blocks.body: A function $f\colon A \to B$ has an inverse if and only if it is a bijection. The inverse is then unique. For real functions, the graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in the line $y = x$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Suppose $g$ is an inverse of $f$. If $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$, then $x_1 = g(f(x_1)) = g(f(x_2)) = x_2$, so $f$ is injective. Every $y \in B$ equals $f(g(y))$, so $f$ is surjective.

Conversely, let $f$ be a bijection. Each $y \in B$ is $f(x)$ for some $x \in A$ (surjectivity), and for only one (injectivity); let $g(y)$ be that $x$. Then $f(g(y)) = y$ by construction, and $g(f(x)) = x$ because $x$ is the only input with output $f(x)$.

If $g$ and $g'$ are both inverses, then for every $y \in B$, $g(y) = g\big(f(g'(y))\big) = g'(y)$. So the inverse is unique.

Finally, $(p, q)$ is on the graph of $f$ exactly when $q = f(p)$, that is, when $p = f^{-1}(q)$, that is, when $(q, p)$ is on the graph of $f^{-1}$. Swapping the coordinates of every point is reflection in the line $y = x$.

blocks.title: Domain, range and inverse of a fraction
blocks.body: Let $f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}$. Find its domain and range, and a formula for $f^{-1}$.
blocks.solution:
The formula makes sense except at $x = 3$, so the domain is $\mathbb R \setminus \{3\}$.

For the range, solve $f(x) = y$:
$$y(x - 3) = 2x + 1 \iff x(y - 2) = 3y + 1.$$
If $y \ne 2$ this gives $x = \dfrac{3y + 1}{y - 2}$, which is not $3$ (otherwise $3y - 6 = 3y + 1$), so it lies in the domain. If $y = 2$ the equation reads $0 = 7$: impossible. So the range is $\mathbb R \setminus \{2\}$.

Each $y \ne 2$ comes from exactly one $x$, so $f$ is a bijection from $\mathbb R \setminus \{3\}$ to $\mathbb R \setminus \{2\}$ with
$$f^{-1}(y) = \frac{3y + 1}{y - 2}.$$
Test: $f(4) = 9$ and $f^{-1}(9) = 28/7 = 4$.

In pictures, $f(x) = 2 + \dfrac{7}{x - 3}$ is $7/x$ moved $3$ right and $2$ up.

blocks.title: Counting solutions with a graph
blocks.body: For each real number $c$, how many real solutions does $|x^2 - 4| = c$ have?

blocks.title: A functional equation
blocks.body: Find all functions $f\colon \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ such that $f(x) + 2f(1 - x) = x^2$ for every real $x$.
blocks.solution:
Replacing $x$ by $1 - x$ gives a second equation in the same unknowns $f(x)$ and $f(1 - x)$:
$$f(1 - x) + 2f(x) = (1 - x)^2.$$
Multiply it by $2$ and subtract the original; the $f(1 - x)$ terms cancel:
$$3f(x) = 2(1 - x)^2 - x^2 = x^2 - 4x + 2, \qquad f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 4x + 2}{3}.$$
So any solution must be this function. Check that it works: since $(1 - x)^2 - 4(1 - x) + 2 = x^2 + 2x - 1$,
$$f(x) + 2f(1 - x) = \frac{(x^2 - 4x + 2) + 2(x^2 + 2x - 1)}{3} = x^2.$$
So there is exactly one such function. The check matters: derived conditions are necessary, not always sufficient.

blocks.body:
- $f^{-1}(x)$ is the inverse function, not $1/f(x)$: for $f(x) = 2x$, $f^{-1}(x) = x/2$ but $1/f(x) = 1/(2x)$.
- $y = f(x - 3)$ is the graph moved right, not left; $g \circ f$ means apply $f$ first.
- Whether an inverse exists depends on the domain. $x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ is not injective, as $(-2)^2 = 2^2$; on $[0, \infty)$ it is a bijection onto $[0, \infty)$ with inverse $\sqrt y$. That is why $\sqrt{x^2} = |x|$.
- The domain is part of the function: $\dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}$ and $x + 1$ differ at $x = 1$, where the first is undefined.

A sequence is a function on the positive integers; the simplest ones are in [[ap-gp]]. The great non-algebraic families are [[exp-log]] and [[trig]], each a bijection after a suitable restriction. Calculus starts with what a function does near a point: [[limits]] and [[continuity]].

Finding an unknown function from an equation it satisfies is an olympiad topic of its own ([[real-functional-eq]], [[integer-functional-eq]]). Bijections are the basic tool of [[counting]], and the functions of linear algebra are the [[linear-maps]].

1. Find the domain and range of $f(x) = \sqrt{4 - x^2}$ and describe its graph.
2. Show that $f(x) = x^3 + x$ is injective on $\mathbb R$. (Hint: factor $f(a) - f(b)$.)
3. For $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 1}{x - 1}$, compute $f(f(x))$. What does the answer tell you about $f^{-1}$?
4. Find all functions $f\colon \mathbb R \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb R$ with $f(x) + 2f(1/x) = 3x$.

entry.sum: The exponential function $a^x$ multiplies its value by the fixed factor $a$ each time $x$ increases by $1$; the logarithm $\log_a$ is its inverse and turns products into sums. The natural base $e \approx 2.71828$ is the one for which the graph of $e^x$ is exactly as steep as it is high.
key: a^{x+y} = a^x a^y, \qquad (a^x)^y = a^{xy}
\log_a(xy) = \log_a x + \log_a y, \qquad \log_a x = \dfrac{\log_b x}{\log_b a}
e = \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1 + \dfrac1n\right)^n \approx 2.71828
entry.why: Growth and decay by a constant factor per unit of time (populations, interest, radioactivity) is exponential, and logarithms measure quantities that span many orders of magnitude, such as the number of digits of a number.

links.note: The prime number theorem says that the number of primes up to $x$ is approximately $x/\ln x$.

Binary search and balanced search trees take about $\log_2 n$ steps on $n$ items, and algorithms are often classified by whether their running time grows logarithmically, polynomially or exponentially.
Radioactive decay and Newton's law of cooling are exponential laws, and the half-life of a decay $e^{-kt}$ is $(\ln 2)/k$.

refs: Maor, e: The Story of a Number

blocks.body:
A colony of bacteria doubles every hour. After $10$ hours it is $2^{10} = 1024$ times larger; after $20$ hours, $2^{20} = 1048576$ times, about a million. Turn the question around: after how many hours is it a billion times larger? That asks for the exponent $x$ with $2^x = 10^9$, and the answer, a little under $30$, is a logarithm.

Exponentials describe anything that grows or shrinks by a fixed factor per unit of time: populations, compound interest, radioactive material. Logarithms answer the inverse question, and they turn multiplication into addition. This lesson builds both functions and explains what is special about the base $e$.

blocks.title: Powers beyond whole numbers
blocks.body:
For a positive integer $n$, $a^n$ means $a \cdot a \cdots a$ with $n$ factors. Counting factors gives two rules:
$$a^{m + n} = a^m a^n, \qquad (a^m)^n = a^{mn}.$$
Everything else is forced if we want these rules to stay true. Take $a > 0$.
- $a^0 \cdot a^n = a^n$ forces $a^0 = 1$.
- $a^{-n} \cdot a^n = a^0 = 1$ forces $a^{-n} = 1/a^n$.
- $(a^{1/q})^q = a$ forces $a^{1/q} = \sqrt[q]{a}$, the positive $q$-th root, and then $a^{p/q} = (\sqrt[q]{a})^p$.

So $8^{2/3} = (\sqrt[3]{8})^2 = 4$ and $4^{-3/2} = 1/8$.

For an irrational exponent such as $\sqrt 2 = 1.41421\ldots$ we approximate. If $a > 1$, the powers $a^{1.4}, a^{1.41}, a^{1.414}, \ldots$ increase, the powers $a^{1.5}, a^{1.42}, a^{1.415}, \ldots$ decrease, and the two lists close in on a single number, which is defined to be $a^{\sqrt 2}$. For $a = 2$: $2^{1.414} \approx 2.6647$ and $2^{1.415} \approx 2.6666$, so $2^{\sqrt 2} \approx 2.665$. Making this rigorous needs [[limits]] and the completeness of the [[real-numbers]]. The outcome is that $a^x$ is defined for every real $x$, and the two rules above remain true for all real exponents.

blocks.title: Exponential function
blocks.body:
Fix a base $a > 0$ with $a \ne 1$. The exponential function with base $a$ is $x \mapsto a^x$, defined for every real $x$. All its values are positive, and every positive number is a value, so its range is $(0, \infty)$. It is increasing if $a > 1$ and decreasing if $0 < a < 1$.

In words: an exponential function multiplies its value by the same factor $a$ every time $x$ increases by $1$.

blocks.title: How fast is exponential growth?
blocks.body:
Compare $n^2$ with $2^n$:
$$\begin{array}{c|cccccccc} n & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 10 & 20 \\ \hline n^2 & 1 & 4 & 9 & 16 & 25 & 36 & 100 & 400 \\ 2^n & 2 & 4 & 8 & 16 & 32 & 64 & 1024 & 1048576 \end{array}$$
After a short contest the exponential wins for good: $2^n > n^2$ for every integer $n \ge 5$. By induction: it holds for $n = 5$, and if $2^n > n^2$ with $n \ge 5$, then $2^{n+1} = 2 \cdot 2^n > 2n^2 \ge (n + 1)^2$, where the last step holds because $2n^2 - (n+1)^2 = (n - 1)^2 - 2 > 0$ for $n \ge 3$.

The same happens against any power, only later: $2^n < n^{10}$ for $2 \le n \le 58$, but $2^n > n^{10}$ from $n = 59$ on. (Once ahead it stays ahead, because each step multiplies $2^n$ by $2$ and $n^{10}$ by only $(1 + 1/n)^{10}$, which is less than $2$ once $n \ge 14$.) Exponential growth with any base $a > 1$ eventually beats every polynomial; such comparisons are the subject of [[asymptotics]].

blocks.title: Logarithm
blocks.body:
Let $a > 0$ with $a \ne 1$, and let $y > 0$. The logarithm of $y$ to the base $a$, written $\log_a y$, is the unique real number $x$ with $a^x = y$.

So $\log_a$ is the inverse function of $x \mapsto a^x$ (see [[functions]]): it answers the question "to what power must I raise $a$ to get $y$?" For example $\log_2 1024 = 10$, $\log_{10} 0.001 = -3$ and $\log_9 3 = \tfrac12$.

blocks.title: Laws of logarithms
blocks.body:
For bases $a, b > 0$ with $a, b \ne 1$, all $x, y > 0$ and every real $r$:
$$\log_a(xy) = \log_a x + \log_a y, \qquad \log_a \frac{x}{y} = \log_a x - \log_a y, \qquad \log_a(x^r) = r\log_a x,$$
$$\log_a x = \frac{\log_b x}{\log_b a} \qquad (\text{change of base}).$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Put $u = \log_a x$ and $v = \log_a y$, so that $x = a^u$ and $y = a^v$. Then $xy = a^u a^v = a^{u + v}$, so $\log_a(xy) = u + v$. In the same way $x/y = a^{u - v}$ and $x^r = (a^u)^r = a^{ru}$, which give the second and third laws.

For the change of base, take $\log_b$ of both sides of $x = a^u$ and use the third law (in base $b$): $\log_b x = u\log_b a$. Since $a \ne 1$ we have $\log_b a \ne 0$, and dividing gives $u = \log_b x / \log_b a$.

blocks.title: The number e
blocks.body:
Which base is best? Base $10$ suits counting digits and base $2$ suits computers, but mathematics has a clear favourite, and compound interest reveals it.

Put $1$ unit in a bank paying 100% interest per year. Paid once, at the end of the year, you finish with $2$. Paid twice, 50% each half-year, you get $(1 + \tfrac12)^2 = 2.25$. Paid $n$ times, each time adding the fraction $\tfrac1n$ of the balance, you get $(1 + \tfrac1n)^n$:
$$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} n & 1 & 2 & 12 & 365 & 1000000 \\ \hline (1 + 1/n)^n & 2 & 2.25 & 2.6130 & 2.7146 & 2.71828 \end{array}$$
The amounts increase but level off. The number they approach is $e = 2.718281828\ldots$, and $\ln x = \log_e x$ is the natural logarithm.

Why is $e$ special? Measure how steeply $a^x$ rises at $x = 0$ by computing $\dfrac{a^h - 1}{h}$ for small $h$:
$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} h & 0.1 & 0.01 & 0.001 \\ \hline (2^h - 1)/h & 0.7177 & 0.6956 & 0.6934 \\ (3^h - 1)/h & 1.1612 & 1.1047 & 1.0992 \\ (e^h - 1)/h & 1.0517 & 1.0050 & 1.0005 \end{array}$$
The slopes at $0$ approach about $0.693$ for base $2$ and about $1.099$ for base $3$ (these are $\ln 2$ and $\ln 3$), while for base $e$ they approach $1$. That the slope of $e^x$ at $0$ is exactly $1$ is proved in [[derivative]] and [[diff-rules]]; the table only suggests it. Since $a^{x + h} - a^x = a^x(a^h - 1)$, the slope of $a^x$ at any point $x$ is $a^x$ times its slope at $0$. So for $e^x$ the slope at every point equals the value: the graph of $e^x$ is exactly as steep as it is high. This is why $e$ and $\ln$ appear throughout calculus.

blocks.title: An exponential equation
blocks.body: Solve $9^x - 4 \cdot 3^x + 3 = 0$.
blocks.solution:
Since $9^x = (3^2)^x = (3^x)^2$, put $u = 3^x$. The equation becomes
$$u^2 - 4u + 3 = (u - 1)(u - 3) = 0,$$
so $u = 1$ or $u = 3$. (Both are positive, as values of $3^x$ must be; a negative root would have to be discarded.) Then $3^x = 1$ gives $x = 0$ and $3^x = 3$ gives $x = 1$. The solutions are $x = 0$ and $x = 1$.

blocks.title: Changing bases
blocks.body: Solve $\log_2 x + \log_4 x + \log_{16} x = 7$.
blocks.solution:
Convert everything to base $2$. Since $\log_2 4 = 2$ and $\log_2 16 = 4$, the change of base formula gives
$$\log_4 x = \frac{\log_2 x}{2}, \qquad \log_{16} x = \frac{\log_2 x}{4}.$$
So the equation is $\left(1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac14\right)\log_2 x = 7$, that is $\tfrac74\log_2 x = 7$, and $\log_2 x = 4$. Hence $x = 16$. Check: $\log_2 16 + \log_4 16 + \log_{16} 16 = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7$.

blocks.title: Counting digits
blocks.body: How many digits does $2^{100}$ have, and what is its first digit? You may use $\log_{10} 2 = 0.30103$ (correct to five decimal places).
blocks.solution:
A positive integer $N$ has $k$ digits exactly when $10^{k-1} \le N < 10^k$, that is, when $k - 1 \le \log_{10} N < k$. So the number of digits is $\lfloor \log_{10} N \rfloor + 1$.

Here $\log_{10} 2^{100} = 100\log_{10} 2$. Since $\log_{10} 2$ is within $0.000005$ of $0.30103$, this lies within $0.0005$ of $30.103$, certainly between $30$ and $31$. So $2^{100}$ has $31$ digits.

For the first digit, write $2^{100} = 10^{30} \cdot 10^{0.103\ldots}$. The factor $10^{0.103\ldots}$ lies between $1$ and $2$, because $0 < 0.103\ldots < \log_{10} 2 = 0.301\ldots$. So $2^{100}$ is between $10^{30}$ and $2 \cdot 10^{30}$, and its first digit is $1$. Indeed
$$2^{100} = 1267650600228229401496703205376.$$

blocks.title: Which is larger?
blocks.body: Which is larger, $99^{100}$ or $100^{99}$?
blocks.solution:
Compare $n^{n+1}$ with $(n + 1)^n$ in general. Dividing both by $n^n$,
$$n^{n+1} > (n + 1)^n \iff n > \left(1 + \frac1n\right)^n.$$
We show $(1 + \tfrac1n)^n < 3$ for every $n \ge 1$. By the binomial theorem,
$$\left(1 + \frac1n\right)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk \frac{1}{n^k}, \qquad \binom nk\frac{1}{n^k} = \frac{1}{k!}\cdot\frac{n}{n}\cdot\frac{n-1}{n}\cdots\frac{n-k+1}{n} \le \frac{1}{k!}.$$
Since $k! \ge 2^{k-1}$ for $k \ge 1$,
$$\left(1 + \frac1n\right)^n \le 1 + \sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{2^{k-1}} = 1 + 2\left(1 - \frac{1}{2^n}\right) < 3.$$
So for every $n \ge 3$ we get $n^{n+1} > (n + 1)^n$. With $n = 99$: $99^{100} > 100^{99}$.

(For $n = 1$ and $n = 2$ the inequality goes the other way: $1 < 2$ and $8 < 9$. The bound also shows that the compound interest amounts in the table never exceed $3$, so $e \le 3$.)

blocks.body:
- $\log(x + y)$ is not $\log x + \log y$; it is the product $xy$ whose logarithm splits. Likewise $(a + b)^x \ne a^x + b^x$ in general.
- Logarithms exist only for positive numbers, so check candidates in the original equation. $\log_2 x + \log_2(x - 2) = 3$ leads to $x(x - 2) = 8$, with roots $4$ and $-2$, but only $x = 4$ is a solution.
- Towers are read from the top down: $2^{3^2} = 2^9 = 512$, while $(2^3)^2 = 64$.
- Real powers $a^x$ need $a > 0$. If the rules held for negative bases we would get $$-2 = (-8)^{1/3} = (-8)^{2/6} = \big((-8)^2\big)^{1/6} = 64^{1/6} = 2$$.
- $\dfrac{\log x}{\log y}$ is not $\log(x/y)$; by the change of base formula it is $\log_y x$.

The slope property of $e^x$ becomes $(e^x)' = e^x$ in [[diff-rules]], and so $y = Ce^{kx}$ solves $y' = ky$, the starting point of [[ode-first]]. The sum $e^x = \sum_{n \ge 0} x^n/n!$ is a [[power-series]], and Euler's formula $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ ties exponentials to [[trig]] through [[complex-numbers]].

In probability, waiting times follow the exponential distribution and the bell curve is a scaled $e^{-x^2/2}$ ([[distributions]]). The [[pnt]] says that there are about $x/\ln x$ primes up to $x$, and reversing $x \mapsto g^x$ modulo a prime is the [[discrete-log]] problem of cryptography.

entry.sum: Cosine and sine are the coordinates of the point $P(\theta)$ reached by travelling a distance $\theta$ around the unit circle from $(1, 0)$; for acute angles they agree with the ratios of sides in a right triangle. The addition formulas, from which most other identities follow, come from the fact that rotations preserve distances.
key: P(\theta) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta), \qquad \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1
\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta
\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta
entry.why: They convert between angles and lengths in triangles, and they are the basic periodic functions, used to describe rotations, oscillations and waves.

links.note: Simple harmonic motion, alternating current and waves are described by sines and cosines of $\omega t$.
Fourier series write a periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines of multiples of a basic frequency.
Euler's formula $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ turns the addition formulas into the rule $e^{i\alpha}e^{i\beta} = e^{i(\alpha + \beta)}$.

blocks.body:
Stand $20$ metres from a tree and look at its top: your line of sight makes an angle of $35^\circ$ with the ground. That is enough to know the height of the tree, about $14$ metres. This link between angles and lengths is trigonometry.

The same functions describe anything that goes round or back and forth, like a wheel or a sound wave. To cover those we extend sine and cosine to all real numbers using a point moving around a circle, and prove the addition formulas, from which nearly every other identity follows.

blocks.title: Right triangles
blocks.body:
Take a right triangle with an acute angle $\theta$. Call the side opposite $\theta$ the opposite side, the other short side the adjacent side, and the longest side the hypotenuse. Two right triangles with the same angle $\theta$ have the same three angles, so they are similar ([[euclid-basics]]) and their side ratios agree. So these ratios depend only on $\theta$:
$$\sin\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \cos\theta = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}.$$
Two triangles give exact values. Half a square, with legs $1$ and hypotenuse $\sqrt 2$, has two $45^\circ$ angles, so $\sin 45^\circ = \cos 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}$. Half an equilateral triangle of side $2$ has hypotenuse $2$, legs $1$ and $\sqrt 3$, and angles $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$; so $\sin 30^\circ = \cos 60^\circ = \tfrac12$ and $\cos 30^\circ = \sin 60^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}$.

For the tree, the height $h$ satisfies $\tan 35^\circ = h/20$, so $h = 20\tan 35^\circ \approx 20 \times 0.700 = 14.0$ metres.

blocks.title: Radians and the unit circle
blocks.body:
Degrees are a convention. The natural measure of an angle is arc length: draw a circle of radius $1$ around the vertex, and the size of the angle is the length of the arc it cuts off. This is radian measure. The whole circle has circumference $2\pi$, so
$$360^\circ = 2\pi, \qquad 180^\circ = \pi, \qquad 90^\circ = \tfrac{\pi}{2}, \qquad 60^\circ = \tfrac{\pi}{3}, \qquad 45^\circ = \tfrac{\pi}{4}, \qquad 30^\circ = \tfrac{\pi}{6},$$
and one radian is $180^\circ/\pi \approx 57.3^\circ$. From now on angles are in radians unless a degree sign is shown.

Now walk anticlockwise a distance $\theta$ along the unit circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, starting at $(1, 0)$. If $0 < \theta < \pi/2$, dropping a perpendicular from the point reached to the $x$-axis gives a right triangle with hypotenuse $1$ and angle $\theta$ at the origin, so the point is $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. We make this the definition for every $\theta$.

blocks.title: Sine and cosine
blocks.body:
For every real number $\theta$, let $P(\theta)$ be the point reached by travelling a distance $\theta$ along the unit circle from $(1, 0)$, anticlockwise for positive $\theta$ and clockwise for negative $\theta$. Then $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$ are the coordinates of this point:
$$P(\theta) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta).$$
Also $\tan\theta = \sin\theta / \cos\theta$ whenever $\cos\theta \ne 0$.

So cosine and sine are the horizontal and vertical positions of a point moving around the unit circle at unit speed.

blocks.title: First properties
blocks.body:
Several facts can be read straight off the circle.

1. $P(\theta)$ is on the unit circle, so $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$; both values lie in $[-1, 1]$.
2. An extra $2\pi$ brings you back to the same point: $\sin(\theta + 2\pi) = \sin\theta$ and $\cos(\theta + 2\pi) = \cos\theta$. Both functions have period $2\pi$.
3. Walking $-\theta$ gives the mirror image of $P(\theta)$ in the $x$-axis: $\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta$ and $\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta$. Cosine is even and sine is odd ([[functions]]).
4. An extra $\pi$ takes you to the opposite point: $\sin(\theta + \pi) = -\sin\theta$ and $\cos(\theta + \pi) = -\cos\theta$. Hence $\tan$ has period $\pi$.
5. Reflection in the line $y = x$ swaps the coordinates, sends $(1, 0)$ to $(0, 1) = P(\pi/2)$ and reverses the direction of travel, so it sends $P(\theta)$ to $P(\pi/2 - \theta)$. Hence $\cos(\tfrac\pi2 - \theta) = \sin\theta$ and $\sin(\tfrac\pi2 - \theta) = \cos\theta$.

The two triangles and these symmetries give the special values:
$$\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc} \theta & 0 & \frac{\pi}{6} & \frac{\pi}{4} & \frac{\pi}{3} & \frac{\pi}{2} & \frac{2\pi}{3} & \pi & \frac{3\pi}{2} & 2\pi \\ \hline \sin\theta & 0 & \frac12 & \frac{\sqrt2}{2} & \frac{\sqrt3}{2} & 1 & \frac{\sqrt3}{2} & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ \cos\theta & 1 & \frac{\sqrt3}{2} & \frac{\sqrt2}{2} & \frac12 & 0 & -\frac12 & -1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}$$
The graph of $\sin$ is a wave of period $2\pi$ between $-1$ and $1$. The graph of $\cos$ is the same wave moved left by $\pi/2$, since $\cos\theta = \sin(\theta + \tfrac\pi2)$ (fact 5 applied to $-\theta$, with fact 3).

blocks.title: Addition formulas
blocks.body:
For all real numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$,
$$\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta, \qquad \cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta,$$
$$\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta, \qquad \sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta.$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Rotate the plane about the origin clockwise by arc length $\beta$. This maps the unit circle to itself and moves each point $P(\theta)$ to $P(\theta - \beta)$; in particular $P(\beta)$ goes to $P(0) = (1, 0)$ and $P(\alpha)$ goes to $P(\alpha - \beta)$. Rotations do not change distances, so the distance from $P(\alpha)$ to $P(\beta)$ equals the distance from $P(\alpha - \beta)$ to $P(0)$. Compute the squares of both with the distance formula, using $\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$:
$$(\cos\alpha - \cos\beta)^2 + (\sin\alpha - \sin\beta)^2 = 2 - 2(\cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta),$$
$$\big(\cos(\alpha - \beta) - 1\big)^2 + \sin^2(\alpha - \beta) = 2 - 2\cos(\alpha - \beta).$$
Setting these equal gives the first formula. Replacing $\beta$ by $-\beta$, and using $\cos(-\beta) = \cos\beta$ and $\sin(-\beta) = -\sin\beta$, gives the second.

For sine, use fact 5 above, $\cos(\tfrac\pi2 - x) = \sin x$ and $\sin(\tfrac\pi2 - x) = \cos x$, together with the first formula:
$$\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\big((\tfrac\pi2 - \alpha) - \beta\big) = \cos(\tfrac\pi2 - \alpha)\cos\beta + \sin(\tfrac\pi2 - \alpha)\sin\beta = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta.$$
Replacing $\beta$ by $-\beta$ gives the last formula.

blocks.title: Consequences: double angles and triangles
blocks.body:
Putting $\beta = \alpha$ gives the double-angle formulas
$$\sin 2\alpha = 2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha, \qquad \cos 2\alpha = \cos^2\alpha - \sin^2\alpha = 2\cos^2\alpha - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2\alpha.$$
Solved for $\cos^2\alpha$ and $\sin^2\alpha$, the last two read $\cos^2\alpha = \tfrac{1 + \cos 2\alpha}{2}$ and $\sin^2\alpha = \tfrac{1 - \cos 2\alpha}{2}$, which let you halve angles. For example $\cos^2\tfrac\pi8 = \tfrac12\big(1 + \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\big)$, so $\cos\tfrac\pi8 = \tfrac12\sqrt{2 + \sqrt 2}$.

Back to triangles. In a triangle $ABC$ write $a = BC$, $b = CA$, $c = AB$, and let $C$ also denote the angle at $C$. Place $C$ at the origin and $A$ at $(b, 0)$, with $B$ above the $x$-axis. Then $B$ is at distance $a$ from the origin in the direction at angle $C$ to the positive $x$-axis: $B = (a\cos C, a\sin C)$. The distance formula gives the law of cosines:
$$c^2 = (a\cos C - b)^2 + a^2\sin^2 C = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C.$$
When $C = \pi/2$ this is Pythagoras' theorem. The same coordinates show that the height from $B$ is $a\sin C$, so the area is $\tfrac12 ab\sin C$. Writing the area in the three possible ways and dividing by $\tfrac12 abc$ gives the law of sines:
$$\frac{\sin A}{a} = \frac{\sin B}{b} = \frac{\sin C}{c}.$$

blocks.title: Exact values
blocks.body: Find $\cos 15^\circ$, $\sin 15^\circ$ and $\tan 15^\circ$ exactly.
blocks.solution:
Write $15^\circ = 45^\circ - 30^\circ$ and use the subtraction formulas:
$$\cos 15^\circ = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac12 = \frac{\sqrt6 + \sqrt2}{4}, \qquad \sin 15^\circ = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} - \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac12 = \frac{\sqrt6 - \sqrt2}{4}.$$
Then
$$\tan 15^\circ = \frac{\sqrt6 - \sqrt2}{\sqrt6 + \sqrt2} = \frac{(\sqrt6 - \sqrt2)^2}{6 - 2} = \frac{8 - 2\sqrt{12}}{4} = 2 - \sqrt3.$$
As a sanity check, $\cos 15^\circ \approx 0.9659$, close to $1$ as it should be for a small angle.

blocks.title: A trigonometric equation
blocks.body: Find all $x$ in $[0, 2\pi)$ with $2\sin^2 x - \sin x - 1 = 0$.
blocks.solution:
This is a quadratic in $s = \sin x$: $2s^2 - s - 1 = (2s + 1)(s - 1) = 0$. So $\sin x = 1$ or $\sin x = -\tfrac12$.

On the unit circle, $\sin x = 1$ only at the top, $x = \tfrac\pi2$. Height $-\tfrac12$ is reached at the mirror images in the $x$-axis of the points at $\tfrac\pi6$ and $\tfrac{5\pi}6$, that is, at $x = \tfrac{11\pi}{6}$ and $x = \tfrac{7\pi}{6}$.

The solutions are $\tfrac\pi2$, $\tfrac{7\pi}6$ and $\tfrac{11\pi}6$; on all of $\mathbb R$, add any multiple of $2\pi$ to these.

blocks.title: Adding two waves
blocks.body: Find the largest value of $3\sin x + 4\cos x$.
blocks.solution:
Factor out $5 = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2}$:
$$3\sin x + 4\cos x = 5\left(\tfrac35\sin x + \tfrac45\cos x\right).$$
Since $(\tfrac35)^2 + (\tfrac45)^2 = 1$, the point $(\tfrac35, \tfrac45)$ lies on the unit circle, so it is $P(\varphi)$ for some angle $\varphi$: $\cos\varphi = \tfrac35$ and $\sin\varphi = \tfrac45$. By the addition formula,
$$3\sin x + 4\cos x = 5(\sin x\cos\varphi + \cos x\sin\varphi) = 5\sin(x + \varphi).$$
This is at most $5$, and equals $5$ when $x = \tfrac\pi2 - \varphi$ (there $\sin x = \tfrac35$, $\cos x = \tfrac45$, and $3 \cdot \tfrac35 + 4 \cdot \tfrac45 = 5$). The maximum is $5$.

The same argument shows that $a\sin x + b\cos x$ is a single wave of amplitude $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.

blocks.title: A product of cosines
blocks.body: Prove that $\cos\dfrac{\pi}{7}\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{7}\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{7} = -\dfrac18$.
blocks.solution:
Call the product $Q$ and put $s = \sin\tfrac\pi7$, which is not $0$. The angles double from one factor to the next, which suggests using $2\sin t\cos t = \sin 2t$ repeatedly:
$$8sQ = 4\Big(2\sin\tfrac\pi7\cos\tfrac\pi7\Big)\cos\tfrac{2\pi}7\cos\tfrac{4\pi}7 = 2\Big(2\sin\tfrac{2\pi}7\cos\tfrac{2\pi}7\Big)\cos\tfrac{4\pi}7 = 2\sin\tfrac{4\pi}7\cos\tfrac{4\pi}7 = \sin\tfrac{8\pi}7.$$
Now $\sin\tfrac{8\pi}{7} = \sin(\pi + \tfrac\pi7) = -\sin\tfrac\pi7 = -s$. So $8sQ = -s$, and dividing by $s \ne 0$ gives $Q = -\tfrac18$.

The same trick shows $\cos 20^\circ\cos 40^\circ\cos 80^\circ = \tfrac18$: there the last step gives $\sin 160^\circ = \sin 20^\circ$, with a plus sign.

blocks.body:
- Calculus formulas, such as the slope of $\sin$ at $0$ being $1$, hold only in radians; check your calculator's mode.
- $\sin(\alpha + \beta) \ne \sin\alpha + \sin\beta$ in general: with $\alpha = \beta = \pi/2$ the left side is $0$ and the right side is $2$.
- $\sin^2 x$ means $(\sin x)^2$, but $\sin^{-1}x$ usually means $\arcsin x$, not $1/\sin x$.
- $\sin x = \tfrac12$ has infinitely many solutions, $x = \tfrac\pi6 + 2k\pi$ and $x = \tfrac{5\pi}6 + 2k\pi$ for integers $k$; a calculator's $\arcsin$ returns only the one in $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$.
- Dividing an equation by $\sin x$ or $\cos x$ loses the solutions where it is zero. Factor instead: $\sin 2x = \sin x$ becomes $\sin x\,(2\cos x - 1) = 0$.

With complex numbers, $P(\theta)$ becomes $\cos\theta + i\sin\theta = e^{i\theta}$, and the addition formulas say that multiplying two such numbers adds their angles ([[complex-numbers]]). The dot product of two vectors is $|\mathbf u||\mathbf v|\cos\theta$, proved from the law of cosines above ([[vectors-plane]]). Comparing areas in the unit circle gives $\sin x / x \to 1$ ([[limits]]), from which $(\sin x)' = \cos x$ follows ([[diff-rules]]); then $\sin$ and $\cos$ solve $y'' = -y$, the equation of a vibrating spring ([[ode-linear]]).

Writing periodic functions as sums of sines and cosines is [[fourier-poisson]]. In olympiad geometry the laws of sines and cosines are standard tools ([[triangle-centres]]).

entry.sum: An arithmetic progression adds a fixed difference $d$ at each step; a geometric progression multiplies by a fixed ratio $r$. Their sums have closed forms, found by pairing terms from the two ends (arithmetic) or by multiplying by $r$ and subtracting (geometric), and a geometric series with $|r| < 1$ has a finite sum even with infinitely many terms.
key: a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d, \qquad a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n = \dfrac{n(a_1 + a_n)}{2}
b_n = b_1 r^{n-1}, \qquad b_1 + b_1 r + \cdots + b_1 r^{n-1} = b_1\dfrac{1 - r^n}{1 - r} \quad (r \ne 1)
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} b_1 r^k = \dfrac{b_1}{1 - r} \quad (|r| < 1)
entry.why: They model steady additive and multiplicative change, such as instalments, interest and repeated halving, and the geometric series is the benchmark against which other infinite series are compared.

links.note: Dirichlet's theorem says that an arithmetic progression $a, a + d, a + 2d, \ldots$ with $\gcd(a, d) = 1$ contains infinitely many primes.

Van der Waerden's theorem gives arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions inside one colour class of any colouring of the positive integers with finitely many colours, and Szemerédi's theorem gives them in every set of positive upper density.
The ratio and root tests decide the convergence of many series by comparing them with a geometric series.

blocks.body:
A theatre has $20$ seats in the front row, and each row has $2$ more seats than the one in front. How many seats are in $30$ rows? A ball bounces back to two thirds of its previous height each time; how far does it travel before it comes to rest? Each question involves numbers made by repeating one step: adding the same amount each time, or multiplying by the same factor.

These are the simplest sequences there are, and the formulas for their sums are among the most used in mathematics.

blocks.title: Arithmetic progression
blocks.body:
A sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ is an arithmetic progression if the difference between consecutive terms is constant: $a_{n+1} - a_n = d$ for every $n$. The number $d$ is the common difference.

So each term is the previous one plus the same number $d$: for example $3, 7, 11, 15, \ldots$ with $d = 4$, or $10, 7, 4, 1, -2, \ldots$ with $d = -3$.

blocks.title: Geometric progression
blocks.body:
A sequence $b_1, b_2, b_3, \ldots$ is a geometric progression if each term is the previous one multiplied by a fixed number $r$: $b_{n+1} = r\,b_n$ for every $n$. The number $r$ is the common ratio.

For example $3, 6, 12, 24, \ldots$ with $r = 2$; $81, 27, 9, 3, 1, \tfrac13, \ldots$ with $r = \tfrac13$; or $1, -1, 1, -1, \ldots$ with $r = -1$.

blocks.title: The general term
blocks.body:
To get from $a_1$ to $a_n$ you add $d$ exactly $n - 1$ times, and to get from $b_1$ to $b_n$ you multiply by $r$ exactly $n - 1$ times:
$$a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d, \qquad b_n = b_1 r^{n-1}.$$
(A formal proof is a one-line induction on $n$.) A sequence is a function on the positive integers ([[functions]]): an arithmetic progression is a linear function of $n$, with the points $(n, a_n)$ on a line of slope $d$, and a geometric progression with positive terms is an exponential function of $n$ ([[exp-log]]).

Three numbers $x, y, z$ are consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression exactly when $y - x = z - y$, that is, $y = \tfrac{x + z}{2}$: the middle term is the arithmetic mean of its neighbours. Three nonzero numbers are consecutive terms of a geometric progression exactly when $y/x = z/y$, that is, $y^2 = xz$; for positive terms the middle one is the geometric mean $\sqrt{xz}$.

blocks.title: Sum of an arithmetic progression
blocks.body:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic progression is
$$S_n = a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n = \frac{n(a_1 + a_n)}{2} = \frac{n\big(2a_1 + (n - 1)d\big)}{2}.$$
In words: the number of terms times the average of the first and the last.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Write the sum twice, once forwards and once backwards, and add the two lines column by column:
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n, \\ S_n &= a_n + a_{n-1} + \cdots + a_1. \end{aligned}$$
The $k$-th column contains $$a_k + a_{n+1-k} = \big(a_1 + (k - 1)d\big) + \big(a_1 + (n - k)d\big) = 2a_1 + (n - 1)d = a_1 + a_n$$, the same for every column. There are $n$ columns, so $2S_n = n(a_1 + a_n)$. Substituting $a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d$ gives the second form.

blocks.title: Sum of a geometric progression
blocks.body:
If $r \ne 1$, the sum of the first $n$ terms of a geometric progression is
$$b_1 + b_1 r + \cdots + b_1 r^{n-1} = b_1\,\frac{1 - r^n}{1 - r} = b_1\,\frac{r^n - 1}{r - 1}.$$
If $r = 1$ the sum is simply $n b_1$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Let $G = 1 + r + r^2 + \cdots + r^{n-1}$. Multiplying by $r$ shifts every term one place along:
$$rG = r + r^2 + \cdots + r^{n-1} + r^n.$$
Subtracting, everything cancels except the two ends: $G - rG = 1 - r^n$. Since $r \ne 1$ we may divide by $1 - r$: $G = \dfrac{1 - r^n}{1 - r}$. Multiply by $b_1$. (The second form is the first with top and bottom multiplied by $-1$.) If $r = 1$, all $n$ terms equal $b_1$.

blocks.title: Sums in practice
blocks.body:
Gauss's sum: $1 + 2 + \cdots + 100 = \tfrac{100 \cdot 101}{2} = 5050$. The theatre: row $30$ has $20 + 29 \cdot 2 = 78$ seats, so $30$ rows hold $\tfrac{30(20 + 78)}{2} = 1470$ seats.

The chessboard legend puts $1$ grain of rice on the first square, $2$ on the second, $4$ on the third, doubling each time. The total over $64$ squares is
$$1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots + 2^{63} = 2^{64} - 1 = 18446744073709551615,$$
far more rice than has ever been grown. In general $1 + 2 + \cdots + 2^{n-1} = 2^n - 1$; in binary, the number written with $n$ ones, plus $1$, is a $1$ followed by $n$ zeros.

Money growing at 5% a year is multiplied by $1.05$ each year, so after $n$ years it is $1.05^n$ times the start. It has doubled once $1.05^n \ge 2$, that is, $n \ge \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.05} \approx 14.2$: after $15$ years.

blocks.title: Infinite geometric series
blocks.body:
Walk halfway to a wall, then half the remaining distance, and so on. After $n$ steps you have covered
$$\frac12 + \frac14 + \cdots + \frac1{2^n} = 1 - \frac1{2^n}.$$
No finite number of steps reaches the wall, but the gap $1/2^n$ becomes as small as you like. We say that the infinite sum equals $1$.

In general, if $|r| < 1$ then $r^n$ shrinks towards $0$. (For $0 < |r| < 1$ write $1/|r| = 1 + t$ with $t > 0$; the binomial theorem gives $(1 + t)^n \ge 1 + nt$, so $|r|^n \le \tfrac{1}{1 + nt}$, which is tiny for large $n$.) So the partial sums $b_1\frac{1 - r^n}{1 - r}$ approach $\dfrac{b_1}{1 - r}$, and we write
$$b_1 + b_1 r + b_1 r^2 + \cdots = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} b_1 r^k = \frac{b_1}{1 - r} \qquad (|r| < 1).$$
If $|r| \ge 1$ and $b_1 \ne 0$, the terms do not shrink to $0$ and the partial sums settle on no number. What "approach" means precisely is the subject of [[seq-limits]] and [[series]].

The bouncing ball, dropped from $3$ metres, rises $2$ m, falls $2$ m, rises $\tfrac43$ m, falls $\tfrac43$ m, and so on. Its total distance is
$$3 + 2\left(2 + \frac43 + \frac89 + \cdots\right) = 3 + 2\cdot\frac{2}{1 - \frac23} = 15 \text{ metres}.$$
Repeating decimals are geometric series too:
$$0.\overline{27} = \frac{27}{100} + \frac{27}{100^2} + \cdots = \frac{27/100}{1 - 1/100} = \frac{27}{99} = \frac{3}{11}, \qquad 0.\overline{9} = \frac{9/10}{1 - 1/10} = 1.$$

blocks.title: An arithmetic progression from two terms
blocks.body: The $5$th term of an arithmetic progression is $17$ and the $12$th term is $45$. Find the sum of the first $20$ terms.
blocks.solution:
Going from the $5$th to the $12$th term adds $d$ seven times, so $7d = 45 - 17 = 28$ and $d = 4$. Then $a_1 = a_5 - 4d = 17 - 16 = 1$, and $a_{20} = 1 + 19 \cdot 4 = 77$. Hence
$$S_{20} = \frac{20(1 + 77)}{2} = 780.$$

blocks.title: Counting the terms
blocks.body: Find the sum of all three-digit multiples of $7$.
blocks.solution:
The smallest three-digit multiple of $7$ is $105 = 7 \cdot 15$ and the largest is $994 = 7 \cdot 142$. The terms are $7k$ for $k = 15, 16, \ldots, 142$, so there are $142 - 15 + 1 = 128$ of them; equivalently $\tfrac{994 - 105}{7} + 1 = 128$. They form an arithmetic progression with difference $7$, so the sum is
$$\frac{128(105 + 994)}{2} = 64 \cdot 1099 = 70336.$$
The $+1$ in the count is the most common error in such problems.

blocks.title: An arithmetic-geometric sum
blocks.body: Find a closed form for $S = 1\cdot 2 + 2\cdot 2^2 + 3\cdot 2^3 + \cdots + n\cdot 2^n$.
blocks.solution:
Each term is an arithmetic progression times a geometric one, and the multiply-and-subtract trick still works. Multiply by the ratio $2$:
$$2S = 1\cdot 2^2 + 2\cdot 2^3 + \cdots + (n - 1)\cdot 2^n + n\cdot 2^{n+1}.$$
Subtract $S$, matching the terms with the same power of $2$. For each power $2^k$ with $2 \le k \le n$ the coefficient becomes $(k - 1) - k = -1$, the term $1\cdot 2$ of $S$ has no partner, and $n\cdot 2^{n+1}$ survives:
$$2S - S = n\cdot 2^{n+1} - (2 + 2^2 + \cdots + 2^n) = n\cdot 2^{n+1} - (2^{n+1} - 2).$$
So $S = (n - 1)2^{n+1} + 2$. Check: $n = 1$ gives $2$, and $n = 2$ gives $2 + 8 = 10 = 1 \cdot 8 + 2$.

blocks.title: Squares in an arithmetic progression
blocks.body: An infinite arithmetic progression of integers with common difference $d > 0$ contains a perfect square. Prove that it contains infinitely many perfect squares.
blocks.solution:
Suppose $x^2$ is a term; we may take $x \ge 0$, since $x^2 = (-x)^2$. Every number of the form $x^2 + md$ with an integer $m \ge 0$ is also a term, namely the one $m$ places further on. Now
$$(x + d)^2 = x^2 + d(2x + d),$$
and $m = 2x + d$ is a positive integer, so $(x + d)^2$ is a later term. Repeating the argument with $x + d$ in place of $x$ shows that $(x + 2d)^2, (x + 3d)^2, \ldots$ are all terms. These squares are increasing, hence all different, so there are infinitely many.

The hypothesis that one square occurs cannot be dropped: $2, 5, 8, 11, \ldots$ contains no squares, because every term leaves remainder $2$ on division by $3$ while every square leaves remainder $0$ or $1$ ([[congruences]]).

blocks.body:
- Off by one: the $n$-th term is $a_1 + (n - 1)d$, not $a_1 + nd$, and from $p$ to $q$ in steps of $d$ there are $\tfrac{q - p}{d} + 1$ terms. A $10$-metre fence with a post every metre has $11$ posts.
- The formula $b_1\frac{1 - r^n}{1 - r}$ does not apply when $r = 1$; then the sum is $nb_1$.
- $\tfrac{b_1}{1 - r}$ is valid only for $|r| < 1$. With $r = 2$ it gives the nonsense $1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots = -1$.
- With $r < 0$ the terms alternate in sign, and the middle term is not $\sqrt{xz}$: in $1, -2, 4$ it is $-\sqrt{1\cdot 4}$.

More general recurrences, such as $a_{n+1} = 2a_n + 1$, are treated in [[sequences]]. The geometric series is the model for all [[series]] and [[power-series]]: the ratio and root tests compare other series with it, and $\tfrac{1}{1 - x} = 1 + x + x^2 + \cdots$ is the first identity of [[generating-functions]].

Arithmetic progressions are central in number theory and combinatorics. Dirichlet proved that $a, a + d, a + 2d, \ldots$ (with $d \ge 1$) contains infinitely many primes whenever $\gcd(a, d) = 1$ ([[l-functions]]); Szemerédi proved that every set of positive integers of positive upper density contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, and Green and Tao proved the same for the primes ([[arithmetic-progressions]]).

entry.sum: A vector is a quantity with a length and a direction, written in coordinates as a pair or triple of numbers and added component by component. The dot product $\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = |\mathbf u||\mathbf v|\cos\theta$ measures angles and is zero exactly for perpendicular vectors; in space, the cross product is a vector perpendicular to both factors whose length is the area of the parallelogram they span.
key: \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 + u_3v_3 = |\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf v|\cos\theta
|\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v| \le |\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf v|, \qquad |\mathbf u + \mathbf v| \le |\mathbf u| + |\mathbf v|
\mathbf u \times \mathbf v = (u_2v_3 - u_3v_2,\ u_3v_1 - u_1v_3,\ u_1v_2 - u_2v_1), \qquad |\mathbf u \times \mathbf v| = |\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf v|\sin\theta
entry.why: Vectors describe displacements, velocities and forces, and they turn geometry problems about midpoints, angles and areas into calculations.

links.note: Forces, velocities and fields are vectors; the work done by a force is a dot product and torque is a cross product.
Computer graphics uses dot products for lighting and cross products for surface normals and for deciding which way a triangle faces.
The gradient of a function of several variables is a vector pointing in the direction of steepest increase, and directional derivatives are dot products with it.

blocks.body:
Walk $3$ km east and then $4$ km north. You end up $5$ km from the start, but to say where you are you also need the direction. A quantity with a size and a direction is a vector; displacements, velocities and forces are examples.

Vectors turn geometry into calculation: a midpoint becomes an average and a right angle becomes an equation. This lesson covers vectors in the plane and in space, the dot product, which measures angles, and the cross product, which measures areas.

blocks.title: Vector
blocks.body:
A vector in the plane is an ordered pair of real numbers $\mathbf u = (u_1, u_2)$, and a vector in space is an ordered triple $\mathbf u = (u_1, u_2, u_3)$; the $u_i$ are its components. For points $A$ and $B$, the vector from $A$ to $B$ is the difference of their coordinates, $\overrightarrow{AB} = B - A$. By Pythagoras' theorem the length of $\mathbf u$ is $|\mathbf u| = \sqrt{u_1^2 + u_2^2}$ in the plane and $\sqrt{u_1^2 + u_2^2 + u_3^2}$ in space.

Picture $\mathbf u$ as an arrow. Arrows with the same length and direction are the same vector wherever they start: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \overrightarrow{CD}$ exactly when $ABDC$ is a parallelogram (possibly a flattened one).

blocks.title: Adding and scaling
blocks.body:
Vectors are added, and multiplied by real numbers (scalars), component by component:
$$\mathbf u + \mathbf v = (u_1 + v_1,\ u_2 + v_2), \qquad t\mathbf u = (tu_1,\ tu_2),$$
and likewise with three components. Geometrically, $\mathbf u + \mathbf v$ means: follow $\mathbf u$, then $\mathbf v$ from its tip, so $\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC}$. The vector $t\mathbf u$ has length $|t|\,|\mathbf u|$ and points the same way as $\mathbf u$ if $t > 0$, the opposite way if $t < 0$. The usual rules of algebra, such as $\mathbf u + \mathbf v = \mathbf v + \mathbf u$, hold.

Fix an origin $O$ and identify each point $P$ with its position vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$. Constructions become averages:
- the midpoint of $AB$ is $M = \tfrac12(A + B)$;
- the point $P$ on segment $AB$ with $AP : PB = m : n$ is $P = A + \tfrac{m}{m + n}(B - A) = \dfrac{nA + mB}{m + n}$.

blocks.title: Dot product
blocks.body:
The dot product (or scalar product) of two vectors is the number
$$\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 \quad \text{(plane)}, \qquad \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 + u_3v_3 \quad \text{(space)}.$$
Straight from the formula, $\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf u = |\mathbf u|^2$, $\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \mathbf v \cdot \mathbf u$, $\mathbf u \cdot (\mathbf v + \mathbf w) = \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v + \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf w$ and $(t\mathbf u) \cdot \mathbf v = t(\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v)$.

blocks.title: Dot product and angle
blocks.body:
Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be nonzero vectors and let $\theta \in [0, \pi]$ be the angle between them when drawn from a common point. Then
$$\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = |\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf v|\cos\theta.$$
In particular $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ are perpendicular if and only if $\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = 0$. (Here $\cos$ is the cosine of [[trig]].)

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Draw $\mathbf u = \overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\mathbf v = \overrightarrow{OB}$, so that $\overrightarrow{BA} = \mathbf u - \mathbf v$. Expanding with the rules above,
$$|\mathbf u - \mathbf v|^2 = (\mathbf u - \mathbf v)\cdot(\mathbf u - \mathbf v) = |\mathbf u|^2 + |\mathbf v|^2 - 2\,\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v.$$
If $O, A, B$ form a genuine triangle, the law of cosines at the vertex $O$ (proved in [[trig]], not here) gives
$$|\mathbf u - \mathbf v|^2 = |\mathbf u|^2 + |\mathbf v|^2 - 2|\mathbf u||\mathbf v|\cos\theta.$$
Comparing the two lines gives the formula. If instead $O, A, B$ lie on one line, then $\mathbf v = t\mathbf u$ with $t \ne 0$, and $\theta = 0$ if $t > 0$, $\theta = \pi$ if $t < 0$. Then $\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = t|\mathbf u|^2$, and also $|\mathbf u||\mathbf v|\cos\theta = |\mathbf u| \cdot |t||\mathbf u| \cdot (\pm 1) = t|\mathbf u|^2$.

Finally, for $\theta \in [0, \pi]$, $\cos\theta = 0$ exactly when $\theta = \pi/2$.

blocks.title: Angles, shadows and two inequalities
blocks.body:
The theorem turns angles into arithmetic: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v}{|\mathbf u||\mathbf v|}$. The angle is acute when $\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v > 0$, right when it is $0$ and obtuse when it is negative. If $|\mathbf e| = 1$, then $\mathbf v \cdot \mathbf e = |\mathbf v|\cos\theta$ is the signed length of the shadow of $\mathbf v$ on the line of $\mathbf e$.

Since $|\cos\theta| \le 1$, we get the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $|\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v| \le |\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf v|$ (trivially true if a vector is zero), with equality exactly when one vector is a multiple of the other. Written out in coordinates it is an inequality about six arbitrary real numbers, here obtained from geometry. It gives the triangle inequality:
$$|\mathbf u + \mathbf v|^2 = |\mathbf u|^2 + 2\,\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v + |\mathbf v|^2 \le |\mathbf u|^2 + 2|\mathbf u||\mathbf v| + |\mathbf v|^2 = \big(|\mathbf u| + |\mathbf v|\big)^2,$$
so $|\mathbf u + \mathbf v| \le |\mathbf u| + |\mathbf v|$: one side of a triangle is never longer than the other two together.

blocks.title: The cross product in space
blocks.body:
In space there is a second product, and it produces a vector:
$$\mathbf u \times \mathbf v = (u_2v_3 - u_3v_2,\ u_3v_1 - u_1v_3,\ u_1v_2 - u_2v_1).$$
(The first component uses the indices $2, 3$, the second $3, 1$, the third $1, 2$.) Its main properties are direct computations.

1. $\mathbf u \times \mathbf v$ is perpendicular to both $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$: expand $\mathbf u \cdot (\mathbf u \times \mathbf v)$ and the six products cancel in pairs; the same works for $\mathbf v$.
2. $\mathbf v \times \mathbf u = -\,\mathbf u \times \mathbf v$, and $\mathbf u \times \mathbf u = \mathbf 0$.
3. Lagrange's identity: $|\mathbf u \times \mathbf v|^2 = |\mathbf u|^2|\mathbf v|^2 - (\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v)^2$. For nonzero vectors the theorem turns the right side into $|\mathbf u|^2|\mathbf v|^2(1 - \cos^2\theta)$, so
$$|\mathbf u \times \mathbf v| = |\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf v|\sin\theta,$$
the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ (base $|\mathbf u|$, height $|\mathbf v|\sin\theta$).

Of the two directions perpendicular to $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$, the cross product takes the one given by the right-hand rule. With $\mathbf i = (1, 0, 0)$, $\mathbf j = (0, 1, 0)$, $\mathbf k = (0, 0, 1)$: $\mathbf i \times \mathbf j = \mathbf k$, $\mathbf j \times \mathbf k = \mathbf i$, $\mathbf k \times \mathbf i = \mathbf j$.

blocks.title: An angle in space
blocks.body: Find the angle between $\mathbf u = (1, 1, 0)$ and $\mathbf v = (0, 1, 1)$.
blocks.solution:
$\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = 0 + 1 + 0 = 1$ and $|\mathbf u| = |\mathbf v| = \sqrt 2$, so
$$\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2} = \frac12, \qquad \theta = \frac\pi3 = 60^\circ.$$
Check: the triangle with vertices $O$, $(1, 1, 0)$, $(0, 1, 1)$ has all sides $\sqrt 2$, so it is equilateral.

blocks.title: Area of a triangle in space
blocks.body: Find the area of the triangle with vertices $A = (1, 0, 0)$, $B = (0, 2, 0)$ and $C = (0, 0, 3)$, and the equation of the plane through them.
blocks.solution:
The sides from $A$ are $\overrightarrow{AB} = (-1, 2, 0)$ and $\overrightarrow{AC} = (-1, 0, 3)$, and
$$\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = \big(2\cdot 3 - 0\cdot 0,\ 0\cdot(-1) - (-1)\cdot 3,\ (-1)\cdot 0 - 2\cdot(-1)\big) = (6, 3, 2),$$
of length $\sqrt{36 + 9 + 4} = 7$. That is the area of the parallelogram on $AB$ and $AC$, so the triangle has area $\tfrac72$.

The vector $\mathbf n = (6, 3, 2)$ is perpendicular to the plane, so $X$ lies in the plane exactly when $\overrightarrow{AX} \cdot \mathbf n = 0$, that is, $6(x - 1) + 3y + 2z = 0$, or $6x + 3y + 2z = 6$. All three vertices satisfy it.

blocks.title: The medians meet
blocks.body: Prove that the three medians of a triangle pass through one point, and that this point divides each median in the ratio $2 : 1$ from the vertex.
blocks.solution:
Let $G = \tfrac13(A + B + C)$. The median from $A$ joins $A$ to the midpoint $M_A = \tfrac12(B + C)$ of $BC$. By the section formula with $m = 2$, $n = 1$, the point dividing $AM_A$ in the ratio $2 : 1$ is
$$\frac{1\cdot A + 2\cdot M_A}{3} = \frac{A + B + C}{3} = G.$$
$G$ is symmetric in $A, B, C$, so the medians from $B$ and $C$ give the same point. Hence all three medians pass through $G$, the centroid, which divides each in the ratio $2 : 1$.

blocks.title: Perpendicular diagonals
blocks.body: Let $A, B, C, D$ be four points in space, not necessarily in one plane, with $A \ne C$ and $B \ne D$. Prove that $AC \perp BD$ if and only if $AB^2 + CD^2 = BC^2 + DA^2$.
blocks.solution:
Treat the points as position vectors and expand each square with $|X - Y|^2 = X\cdot X - 2X\cdot Y + Y\cdot Y$. In
$$AB^2 + CD^2 - BC^2 - DA^2 = |B - A|^2 + |D - C|^2 - |C - B|^2 - |A - D|^2$$
each of $A\cdot A$, $B\cdot B$, $C\cdot C$, $D\cdot D$ appears once with each sign and cancels, leaving
$$-2A\cdot B - 2C\cdot D + 2B\cdot C + 2A\cdot D = 2(A - C)\cdot(D - B) = 2\,\overrightarrow{CA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BD}.$$
So the condition holds exactly when $\overrightarrow{CA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BD} = 0$, that is, when the directions of $AC$ and $BD$ are perpendicular (in space the lines need not meet). For a plane quadrilateral $ABCD$: the diagonals are perpendicular exactly when the sums of squares of opposite sides are equal.

blocks.body:
- You cannot cancel in a dot product: $\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf w$ only says that $\mathbf u$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf v - \mathbf w$. With $\mathbf u = (1, 0)$, $\mathbf v = (0, 1)$, $\mathbf w = (0, 2)$ both products are $0$.
- The cross product is defined only in space. It is not commutative, and not associative: $(\mathbf i \times \mathbf i) \times \mathbf j = \mathbf 0$, but $\mathbf i \times (\mathbf i \times \mathbf j) = \mathbf i \times \mathbf k = -\mathbf j$.
- The sum $A + B$ of two points depends on the choice of origin; combinations with coefficients adding up to $1$, like the midpoint $\tfrac12 A + \tfrac12 B$, do not.

In linear algebra, maps respecting addition and scaling are given by [[matrices]], objects obeying the same rules form [[vector-spaces]], and the dot product generalises to [[inner-products]]. The cross product is a $3 \times 3$ [[determinants|determinant]] in disguise, and $|\mathbf u \cdot (\mathbf v \times \mathbf w)|$ is the volume of the box spanned by three vectors.

Cauchy–Schwarz for $n$ numbers is in [[cauchy-schwarz]], and vector methods in olympiad geometry in [[analytic-geometry]]. In calculus, the direction of steepest increase of a function of several variables is a vector, the gradient ([[partial-derivatives]]).

1. For which $t$ are $(1, t, 2)$ and $(t, 3, -4)$ perpendicular?
2. Find a nonzero vector perpendicular to both $(1, 2, 3)$ and $(4, 5, 6)$.
3. Prove with vectors that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
4. Show that $|\mathbf u + \mathbf v|^2 + |\mathbf u - \mathbf v|^2 = 2|\mathbf u|^2 + 2|\mathbf v|^2$, and say what this means for a parallelogram.

entry.sum: $\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L$ means that $f(x)$ is as close to $L$ as you like for all $x$ close enough to $a$, with $x \ne a$; the value of $f$ at $a$ plays no role. The epsilon–delta definition makes this precise, and the limit laws and the squeeze theorem do most of the computing.
key: \lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L \iff \forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists \delta > 0:\ 0 < |x - a| < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon
\lim_{x\to a}\big(f(x) + g(x)\big) = L + M, \qquad \lim_{x\to a} f(x)g(x) = LM
\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin x}{x} = 1
entry.why: Derivatives, integrals, continuity and infinite sums are all defined as limits, so this is the idea on which the whole of calculus rests.

links.note: Real analysis is built on the epsilon–delta definition, extending it to sequences, series and uniform convergence of functions.
The law of large numbers and the central limit theorem are limit statements about averages of many random variables.
Running times of algorithms are compared through limits of ratios as the input size tends to infinity.

refs: Courant & John, Introduction to Calculus and Analysis, Volume I

blocks.body:
What is $\dfrac{\sqrt{x + 9} - 3}{x}$ at $x = 0$? Substituting gives $\tfrac00$, which means nothing. Yet for $x$ near $0$ the values crowd around one number. That number is the limit: not the value at the point, but the value the function is heading for.

Slopes, instantaneous speeds and areas under curves are all limits. This lesson starts with tables, gives the precise definition, and ends with $\sin x / x \to 1$.

blocks.title: Watching values approach
blocks.body:
Let $f(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x + 9} - 3}{x}$ for $x \ge -9$, $x \ne 0$. Near $0$, to five decimals:
$$\begin{array}{c|cccccc} x & -0.1 & -0.01 & -0.001 & 0.001 & 0.01 & 0.1 \\ \hline f(x) & 0.16713 & 0.16671 & 0.16667 & 0.16666 & 0.16662 & 0.16621 \end{array}$$
From both sides the values approach $0.1666\ldots = \tfrac16$. Algebra confirms this: multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt{x + 9} + 3$,
$$f(x) = \frac{(x + 9) - 9}{x\big(\sqrt{x + 9} + 3\big)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 9} + 3} \qquad (x \ne 0),$$
and as $x$ approaches $0$ the right side approaches $\tfrac{1}{3 + 3} = \tfrac16$. We write $\lim_{x\to 0} f(x) = \tfrac16$.

Note that $f$ is not defined at $0$, and that does not matter: the limit looks at $x$ near $0$, never at $0$ itself. Changing or removing the value at $0$ never changes the limit.

blocks.title: When there is no limit
blocks.body:
A limit must be a single number, approached from both sides. Three things can go wrong.

1. A jump. $s(x) = |x|/x$ is $1$ for $x > 0$ and $-1$ for $x < 0$. The one-sided limits are $\lim_{x\to 0^+} s(x) = 1$ and $\lim_{x\to 0^-} s(x) = -1$; since they differ, $\lim_{x\to 0} s(x)$ does not exist.
2. Blowing up. As $x \to 0$, $1/x^2$ grows beyond every bound. The notation $\lim_{x\to 0} 1/x^2 = \infty$ is shorthand for this way of failing; $\infty$ is not a number.
3. Oscillation. On every interval $(0, \delta)$, $1/x$ runs through infinitely many periods of the sine, so $\sin(1/x)$ takes every value in $[-1, 1]$ there. It approaches nothing.

blocks.title: Limit
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be defined on an open interval around $a$, except possibly at $a$ itself. We say that $f(x)$ tends to $L$ as $x$ tends to $a$, and write $\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L$, if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that
$$0 < |x - a| < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon.$$
In words: however small a tolerance $\varepsilon$ you demand around $L$, every $x$ close enough to $a$ (within $\delta$, but not equal to $a$) gives a value within that tolerance.

blocks.title: The definition as a game
blocks.body:
Think of a game. An opponent names a tolerance $\varepsilon > 0$, as small as they like; you reply with a $\delta > 0$ such that every $x$ with $0 < |x - a| < \delta$ has $f(x)$ within $\varepsilon$ of $L$. The limit is $L$ if you can always reply. Your $\delta$ may depend on $\varepsilon$, but not on $x$.

For $\lim_{x\to 3}(2x + 1) = 7$: since $|(2x + 1) - 7| = 2|x - 3|$, the reply $\delta = \varepsilon/2$ works.

The condition $0 < |x - a|$ makes the value at $a$ irrelevant. For $s(x) = |x|/x$ and any $L$, the tolerance $\varepsilon = 1$ cannot be met: every window around $0$ contains points where $s = 1$ and points where $s = -1$, and no number is within $1$ of both.

blocks.title: Limit laws
blocks.body:
Suppose $\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x\to a} g(x) = M$. Then
$$\lim_{x\to a}\big(f(x) + g(x)\big) = L + M, \qquad \lim_{x\to a} f(x)g(x) = LM,$$
and, if $M \ne 0$, $\lim_{x\to a} \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \dfrac{L}{M}$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
All windows are of the form $0 < |x - a| < \delta$; to meet several conditions at once, take the smallest of the corresponding $\delta$'s.

Sum. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose a window in which $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon/2$ and $|g(x) - M| < \varepsilon/2$. There, by the triangle inequality,
$$|f(x) + g(x) - (L + M)| \le |f(x) - L| + |g(x) - M| < \varepsilon.$$

Product. Write $$f(x)g(x) - LM = f(x)\big(g(x) - M\big) + M\big(f(x) - L\big)$$. Using the tolerance $1$ for $f$, there is a window in which $|f(x) - L| < 1$, so $|f(x)| < |L| + 1$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, shrink the window so that also $|g(x) - M| < \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2(|L| + 1)}$ and $|f(x) - L| < \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2(|M| + 1)}$. Then
$$|f(x)g(x) - LM| \le |f(x)|\,|g(x) - M| + |M|\,|f(x) - L| < \frac\varepsilon2 + \frac\varepsilon2 = \varepsilon.$$

Quotient. By the product law it is enough to show $1/g(x) \to 1/M$. In a window where $|g(x) - M| < |M|/2$ we have $|g(x)| > |M|/2$ (so $g(x) \ne 0$) and
$$\left|\frac{1}{g(x)} - \frac1M\right| = \frac{|M - g(x)|}{|g(x)|\,|M|} < \frac{2|g(x) - M|}{M^2},$$
which is less than $\varepsilon$ once also $|g(x) - M| < \varepsilon M^2/2$.

blocks.title: Using the laws, and limits at infinity
blocks.body:
From $\lim_{x\to a} c = c$ and $\lim_{x\to a} x = a$, the laws give $\lim_{x\to a} P(x) = P(a)$ for every polynomial $P$, and the same for a quotient of polynomials whose denominator is not $0$ at $a$. When top and bottom both tend to $0$ the laws do not apply directly; simplify first, as above.

$\lim_{x\to\infty} f(x) = L$ means: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ with $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ whenever $x > N$. The basic example is $1/x \to 0$ (take $N = 1/\varepsilon$), and the limit laws hold here too. For instance, dividing top and bottom by $x^2$,
$$\frac{3x^2 + 1}{x^2 - 5x} = \frac{3 + 1/x^2}{1 - 5/x} \to \frac{3 + 0}{1 - 0} = 3 \qquad (x \to \infty).$$

blocks.title: Squeeze theorem
blocks.body: Suppose $g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)$ for all $x$ in some window $0 < |x - a| < r$, and $\lim_{x\to a} g(x) = \lim_{x\to a} h(x) = L$. Then $\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $\delta \le r$ so small that $|g(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ and $|h(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ whenever $0 < |x - a| < \delta$. For such $x$,
$$L - \varepsilon < g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x) < L + \varepsilon,$$
so $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$.

blocks.title: A proof from the definition
blocks.body: Prove from the definition that $\lim_{x\to 2} x^2 = 4$.
blocks.solution:
We need $|x^2 - 4| = |x - 2|\,|x + 2|$ to be small. We control $|x - 2|$; the danger is that $|x + 2|$ might be large. So first restrict to $|x - 2| < 1$: then $1 < x < 3$ and $|x + 2| < 5$.

Given $\varepsilon > 0$, let $\delta = \min(1, \varepsilon/5)$. If $0 < |x - 2| < \delta$, then $|x + 2| < 5$ (as $\delta \le 1$) and $|x - 2| < \varepsilon/5$, so
$$|x^2 - 4| = |x - 2|\,|x + 2| < \frac\varepsilon5 \cdot 5 = \varepsilon.$$
(For $\varepsilon = 0.01$, $\delta = 0.002$, and indeed $2.002^2 = 4.008004$.) Taking a minimum is the standard way to impose two requirements on $\delta$.

blocks.title: Simplify first
blocks.body: Compute $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2}\frac{x^3 - 8}{x - 2}$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\left(\sqrt{x^2 + x} - x\right)$.
blocks.solution:
For the first, since $x^3 - 8 = (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4)$, for $x \ne 2$ the quotient equals $x^2 + 2x + 4$, which tends to $12$.

For the second, multiply and divide by $\sqrt{x^2 + x} + x$: for $x > 0$,
$$\sqrt{x^2 + x} - x = \frac{(x^2 + x) - x^2}{\sqrt{x^2 + x} + x} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 1/x} + 1} \to \frac{1}{1 + 1} = \frac12.$$
(At $x = 100$ it is $0.49876\ldots$.) The tempting guess "$\sqrt{x^2 + x} \approx x$, so the limit is $0$" is wrong.

blocks.title: The limit of sin x over x
blocks.body: Prove that $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$, with $x$ in radians. Deduce $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1 - \cos x}{x^2} = \frac12$.
blocks.solution:
This uses the unit-circle definitions of $\sin$, $\cos$ and $\tan$ and the double-angle formula, all from [[trig]].

Take first $0 < x < \pi/2$. On the unit circle with centre $O$, let $A = (1, 0)$, $P = (\cos x, \sin x)$ and $T = (1, \tan x)$, the point where line $OP$ meets the vertical through $A$. The triangle $OAP$ lies inside the circular sector $OAP$, which lies inside the triangle $OAT$. Comparing areas (the sector is the fraction $\tfrac{x}{2\pi}$ of a disc of area $\pi$),
$$\frac12\sin x < \frac12 x < \frac12\tan x.$$
The first inequality gives $\sin x < x$. The second, multiplied by $2\cos x / x > 0$, gives $\cos x < \dfrac{\sin x}{x}$. For a lower bound on $\cos x$, use $1 - \cos x = 2\sin^2\frac x2$ and $\sin\frac x2 < \frac x2$:
$$1 - \cos x = 2\sin^2\frac x2 < 2\left(\frac x2\right)^2 = \frac{x^2}{2}.$$
Altogether
$$1 - \frac{x^2}{2} < \cos x < \frac{\sin x}{x} < 1 \qquad (0 < x < \tfrac\pi2).$$
Every term is unchanged when $x$ is replaced by $-x$, so this holds for $0 < |x| < \tfrac\pi2$, and the squeeze theorem gives $\sin x / x \to 1$.

For the second limit,
$$\frac{1 - \cos x}{x^2} = \frac{2\sin^2(x/2)}{x^2} = \frac12\left(\frac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\right)^2 \to \frac12 \cdot 1^2 = \frac12,$$
by the product law and the first limit with $x/2$ in place of $x$.

blocks.title: A function with only one limit
blocks.body: Let $f(x) = x$ when $x$ is rational and $f(x) = 0$ when $x$ is irrational. Show that $\lim_{x\to 0} f(x) = 0$, but that $\lim_{x\to a} f(x)$ does not exist for any $a \ne 0$.
blocks.solution:
For every $x$, $-|x| \le f(x) \le |x|$, and both bounds tend to $0$, so $f(x) \to 0$ as $x \to 0$ by the squeeze theorem.

Now let $a \ne 0$, suppose $f(x) \to L$ as $x \to a$, and take $\varepsilon = |a|/3$ with its window. Every interval contains rational and irrational numbers ([[real-numbers]]). An irrational $x$ in the window gives $|0 - L| < |a|/3$; a rational $x$ in the window with also $|x - a| < |a|/3$ gives $|x - L| < |a|/3$. Then
$$|a| \le |a - x| + |x - L| + |L| < \frac{|a|}3 + \frac{|a|}3 + \frac{|a|}3 = |a|,$$
which is impossible. So $f$ has a limit at exactly one point.

blocks.body:
- $\tfrac00$ is not automatically $1$: $\tfrac{2x}{x} \to 2$, $\tfrac{x^2}{x} \to 0$, and $\tfrac{x}{x^2}$ has no limit as $x \to 0$, though all three have this form.
- Tables can mislead: $\sin(\pi/x)$ is $0$ at $x = 1, 0.1, 0.01, \ldots$, yet has no limit at $0$.
- "Gets closer and closer" is not the definition: as $x \to 0$, $x^2$ gets ever closer to $-1$, but its limit is $0$.
- The limit laws need both limits to exist: $\sin(1/x) + \big(-\sin(1/x)\big) \to 0$, although neither term has a limit at $0$.

A function whose limit at $a$ equals its value there is continuous ([[continuity]]). The derivative is the limit $\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$ ([[derivative]]), and the area under a curve is a limit of sums of rectangles ([[riemann-integral]]). Many $\tfrac00$ limits yield to [[lhopital]], and growth rates as $x \to \infty$ are compared in [[asymptotics]].

Restricting $x$ to the integers gives limits of sequences ([[seq-limits]]) and [[series]]; the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem are limit statements ([[limit-theorems]]).

2. Prove from the definition that $\lim_{x\to 4}\sqrt x = 2$. (Hint: $\sqrt x - 2 = \frac{x - 4}{\sqrt x + 2}$.)
3. Compute $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin 3x}{x}$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\tan x}{x}$.
4. Does $\lim_{x\to 0} x\sin(1/x)$ exist? Justify your answer.
